title: Near-Surface Microstructure and Properties of High-Carbon Metastable Austenitic Steels Subjected to Abrasive Wear
abstract: Abstract The microstructure and properties in the near-surface region of two high-carbon metastable austenitic steels after two-body abrasive wear were studied. The samples were subjected to wear loads in a range of 8–32 N (corresponding to approximately 0.1–0.4 MPa). Vickers hardness measurements on the worn surface as well as nanoindentation measurements on the cross section present a significant hardness increase from the bulk toward the surface of up to 400%. Electron channeling contrast imaging was utilized to assign the indents from the nanoindentation measurements to the martensitic or austenitic phase. Within a subsurface layer with a thickness of a few microns, it was impossible to distinguish a phase via these images. Magnetic force microscopy revealed a few microns thick martensitic layer, which is the main cause of the significant hardness increase in the near-surface region. No considerable influence of the wear load (within the tested load range) on the resulting microstructure and mechanical properties was found. Transmission electron microscopy images reveal a grain size of several nanometers within the martensitic subsurface layer, which accounts for the observed ductility on the worn surfaces, despite the inherent brittleness typically associated with high-carbon martensite.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Components subjected to severe abrasive wear in industrial applications such as mining, mineral processing, agricultural machinery and bulk material conveying systems require materials that combine high wear resistance with cost effectiveness and, increasingly, sustainability.

Conventional wear-resistant austenitic steels, often exemplified by Hadfield steels, have long been recognized for their exceptional work-hardening capacity and robust performance, particularly in environments characterized by high energy impact wear. These steels typically contain elevated manganese (10–14 wt%) and carbon (1–1.4 wt%) contents, which stabilize the austenitic phase and enables deformation twinning during plastic straining. This results in pronounced work-hardening capabilities and provides excellent wear resistance under high-energy impact conditions [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. This characteristic, combined with good fracture toughness, contributes to their excellent performance. However, under mild wear conditions—where plastic deformation is insufficient to activate work-hardening—conventional Hadfield steels exhibit significantly reduced wear resistance.

To overcome these limitations, recent alloy design strategies have focused on reducing austenite stability by lowering the carbon and/or manganese content in order to activate deformation-induced martensitic transformation as an additional hardening mechanism [ 2 ,  4 ]. Zambrano et al. observed an improved wear resistance with increasing strain-hardening rates associated with a reduction in stacking fault energy [ 5 ], while even higher strain-hardening rates can be achieved when deformation-induced martensite formation is promoted [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. As a consequence, high-carbon metastable austenitic steels (MAS) demonstrated exceptional wear resistance, particularly under dry-sliding abrasive wear conditions [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]. In two-body abrasive loading, these steels have been reported to outperform both conventional martensitic wear steels and austenitic Hadfield steels by factors of up to seven, making them highly attractive candidates for demanding wear applications [ 9 ].

Despite these promising results, the fundamental microstructural mechanisms responsible for the superior wear performance of MAS remain insufficiently understood. While the superior performance MAS is often attributed to deformation-induced martensite formation during wear, the microstructural mechanisms underpinning this behavior remain insufficiently explored. X-ray diffraction (XRD) studies have confirmed partial phase transformation from austenite to martensite after wear [ 9 ,  10 ,  12 ], suggesting a dynamic adaptation of near-surface hardness that contributes to reduced wear rates. However, the special extend and morphology of the transformed martensitic layer is still to be investigated. Early work by Jost et al. [ 4 ] showed martensite nucleation at slip band intersections, consistent with the Olson and Cohen model for deformation-induced martensite formation [ 13 ]. Nevertheless, systematic and high-resolution investigations of the near-surface region—where wear-induced deformation is most severe—are still lacking.

A particularly unresolved issue concerns the ability of the transformed martensitic layer to accommodate significant plastic deformation during wear [ 9 ], despite the known brittleness of high-carbon martensite [ 14 ,  15 ]. This apparent contradiction raises questions about the mechanisms that enable plastic deformation in the martensitic phase under wear conditions.

To address these open questions, the present study employs a combination of high-resolution mechanical and microstructural characterization techniques specifically targeted at the near-surface region of worn high-carbon metastable austenitic steels. Nanoindentation testing is used to probe local hardness and indentation response on the sub-micrometer length scale, providing quantitative insight into the mechanical properties and deformation behavior of both austenite and wear-induced martensite. These measurements are correlated with electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) performed on cross sections from the near-surface region to resolve phase distribution and deformation substructures. Magnetic force microscopy (MFM) is applied to directly visualize the ferromagnetic martensitic layer and, for the first time, to estimate its spatial extent. In addition, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is employed to investigate the near-surface microstructure at high spatial resolution. By integrating these complementary techniques, this study aims to clarify the nature, thickness, and mechanical role of the wear-induced martensitic layer and to provide new insights into the mechanisms governing the exceptional wear resistance of metastable austenitic steels.

sections.heading: Materials and Sample Preparation
paragraphs: The steel designation and chemical composition for the two MAS that have been used in this work are given in Table  1 . The samples have been retrieved from hot-rolled sheets that were fabricated from cast and subsequently forged slabs at COMTES FHT (Czech Republic). The austenitization of the samples was carried out in a muffle furnace continuously purged with inert gas at the temperature  T A  for a given time  t A  (Table  1 ). After austenitization, the samples were quenched in water to room temperature. Table 1 Chemical composition (wt%) and heat treatment details of the MAS, austenitization temperature ( T A ) and time ( t A ) Steel C Mn Si Cr Al T A  (°C) t A  (s) 100 1.01 4.04 1.56 0.52 0.02 950 600 100Al 0.99 4.06 1.52 0.51 1.49 1000 300

The wear samples were obtained by two-body abrasion tests (“Suga abrasion tester NUS-ISO3,” Suga Test Instruments Co. Ltd.). The abrasive wear was generated by pressing SiC abrasive paper (46 µm grit size) against the sample surface with a load of 8–32 N (corresponding to approximately 0.1–0.4 MPa) and simultaneously moving the sample with a relative velocity of 26.7 mm s −1 . The characterization of the worn specimens was performed directly on the worn surface and on the cross sections. To prepare the cross sections, cuts were made perpendicular to the direction of wear through the worn surface using a precision abrasive cutoff saw “Mecatome T210” (PRESI GmbH) and Al 2 O 3  cutting wheel (Cloeren technology). A galvanic nickel coating was applied to protect the surface. The sample was embedded before the cross section was ground and polished up to 0.040 µm SiO 2  OPS suspension (Struers).

sections.heading: Hardness Measurement
paragraphs: The hardness of the near-surface regions was investigated by nanoindentation on the cross sections and Vickers hardness tests on the as-worn surface, as illustrated in Fig.  1 . Vickers hardness was measured using a hardness tester “KB30S” (KB Prüftechnik GmbH). The mean value and standard deviation of five consecutive measurements were calculated. The influence of the surface roughness of the worn surface on the Vickers hardness measurements can be neglected, as only indents with a diagonal ratio between 0.95 and 1.05 were considered. Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of a typical worn sample. The characterized regions are marked

Nanoindentation was performed in continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) mode using a “Nanoindenter G200” (Keysight Technologies) and a Berkovich indenter. Parameters used are given in Table  2 . Before and after each measurement, the indenter geometry and machine stiffness were carefully checked by reference measurements in fused silica. The measurement data in a range between 100 and 200 nm indentation depth were used to calculate the mean indentation hardness from the CSM. Table 2 Parameters used for nanoindentation in continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) mode Parameter Value CSM-frequency (Hz) 45 CSM-amplitude (nm) 2 Stiffness criteria (N m −1 ) 200 Thermal drift rate (nm s −1 )  ≤ 0.05 Indentation depth (nm) 200

To measure the indentation hardness in the near-surface region, three measurement grids were defined. Each grid consisted of eight blocks, and each block contained 20 indents arranged in five rows and four columns. The spacing of the five indentations within a row was set to 2 µm, which corresponds to ten times the indentation depth. The distance in between rows was 4 µm, which corresponds to 20 times the indentation depth. According to recent investigations [ 16 ], the chosen spacing does not lead to any significant influence of the indentation hardness values by overlapping stress fields. With every block, the distance to the surface increases by 0.5 µm. Thus, a total of 480 indents were placed in varying distances from the surface for each sample. To visualize this, Fig.  2  shows an ECCI image including indents arranged in the described structure. As can be seen in the figure, some indentations did not fulfill the required spacing (circled indentations in Fig.  2 ) and were, therefore, not considered for the evaluation. Based on the ECCI images and hardness–displacement curves, the indents were also divided into three categories: (i) indentations in thermal martensite, (ii) indentations in austenite, and (iii) all the indentations that could not confidently be assigned to one of these two phases. This made it possible to determine the hardness profile of austenite and martensite as a function of the surface distance. Fig. 2 Electron channeling contrast image of nanoindents made at the cross section of MAS 100 after wear at 0.2 MPa. The arrangement of the indents in blocks is marked

Figure  3  displays representative load–displacement curves of the distinguished phases. Furthermore, Fig.  4  shows the indentation hardness calculated from the CSM as a function of the displacement. Note that the indentation hardness changes considerably at smaller indentation depths due to the small contact area and, therefore, significant influence of the indenter geometry. The measurements were only evaluated within the specified range (100–200 nm). Fig. 3 Typical load–displacement curves of the nanoindentation measurements. Measurements were taken on cross sections of the MAS 100 after wear at 0.1 MPa Fig. 4 indentation hardness as a function of the displacement into the surface for all considered microstructural constituents. Measurements were taken on cross sections of the MAS 100 after wear at 0.1 MPa

sections.heading: Magnetic Force Microscopy
paragraphs: In this study, MFM was used to image a phase contrast between the paramagnetic austenite and ferromagnetic ferritic phases. The measurements were conducted using a scanning probe microscope “Keysight 5600LS SPM” (Keysight Technologies). MFM probes were purchased from BudgetSensors (“MagneticMulti75M-G”) and NT-MDT Spectrum Instruments (“MFM01”). Standard dynamic two-pass MFM was performed, where the first pass maps the topography and the second pass was used to measure the magnetic information [ 17 ]. Further applied measurement parameters can be found in Table  3 . Table 3 Parameters used for magnetic force microscopy (MFM)-imaging Parameter Value Frequency (kHz) 74–79 Frequency off-set (kHz) −0.1 Amplitude (A) 3–5 P and I-gain (%) 5–15 Scan speed (lines per second) 0.2–1 Image resolution (px per µm) 25.6–51.2 Lift height (nm) 15

sections.heading: Electron Microscopy
paragraphs: A “Gemini Ultra 55plus” (Zeiss) was used for scanning electron microscopy (SEM) investigations utilizing “High Current” mode. The assignment of the indents to the individual phases was based on the phase contrast from ECCI images using an accelerating voltage between 10 and 15 kV, an aperture size of 120 µm and a working distance of 8 mm. A four-quadrant BSE detector was used.

For TEM investigations, a lamella of each sample was prepared using the “Dual FIB” (FEI Helios NanoLab 600i, FEI/Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). To prevent damage to the sample, an electronbeam Pt-layer (~ 60 nm) was deposited on the surface, followed by an ionbeam Pt-layer (1 µm). With 30 kV voltage and 2.5 nA ionbeam current, approximately, 2-µm-thick lamellas were cut from the sample and fixed on a Cu-grid with Pt. The thinning of the lamellas to 50 nm was carried out in several steps (30 kV, 16 kV, 8 kV and 5 kV) while tilting the sample between 50.5° and 53.5°. All lamellas were investigated by TEM (“Neoarm 200F,” JEOL Ltd., Japan) using an accelerating voltage of 200 kV and emission current of 10 µA. Bright Field (BF) images in TEM mode and BF, Annular BF (ABF) and Annular DF (ADF) in the scanning-TEM (STEM) mode were executed to display the structure. Diffraction patterns were recorded using selected area diffraction (SAED) with a spot size of approximately 100–200 nm.

sections.heading: Phase Composition
paragraphs: Figure  5  shows ECCI images of the near-surface cross sections before and after wear at 0.2 MPa. Differences between the two MAS can be observed. Beneath the unassignable layer, a deformation structure (slip bands, mechanical twins) is visible. As for the unassignable layer, the thickness of the deformation layer is larger for the MAS 100 as compared to the MAS 100Al. Fig. 5 Typical ECCI images of the near-surface cross section pre- and post-wear for MAS 100 and MAS 100Al. The post-wear condition was recorded after two-body abrasive wear tests at 0.2 MPa

The MFM map in Fig.  6  reveals a ferromagnetic layer below the abraded surface. The layer—homogeneous in wide areas—extends a few micrometers below the surface. No clear difference can be observed in the extent of the layer depending on the wear load. In some areas, this layer expands into the austenite in tapered, parallel form. Fig. 6 Magnetic force microscopy map of the subsurface after abrasive wear at a wear load of 0.1 MPa. Light colors indicate no cantilever phase shift and, therefore, no magnetic interactions (austenitic phase) and the darker colors indicate a strong negative cantilever phase shift revealing ferromagnetic interaction (martensite). The image was stitched together from three individual images

The corresponding TEM images of the unassignable layer for the two MAS are shown in Fig.  7 . The microstructures of both are characterized by nanometer-sized grains, as evident from the bright-field images. This observation is further supported by the corresponding SAED patterns, which display distinct diffraction rings indicative of a nanocrystalline structure. Fig. 7 TEM images of the subsurface microstructure and the corresponding SAED pattern revealing a nanoscale polycrystalline microstructure. Bright-field TEM image of the  a  MAS 100 sample at 0.4 MPa,  b  MAS 100Al sample at 0.4 MPa, Corresponding SAED pattern of the  c  MAS 100 sample,  d  MAS 100Al sample

sections.heading: Hardness-Depth Profile
paragraphs: Figure  8  displays the Vickers hardness of the MAS 100 and 100Al as measured directly on the as-worn surface (see Fig.  1 ) in relation to the corresponding indentation depth for various wear loads. In each case, the Vickers hardness of the MAS 100 is slightly higher compared to the MAS 100Al. For both MAS, no correlation between the applied wear load and the maximum hardness as well as the hardness profile is found. For indentation depths greater than 10 µm, the Vickers hardness is around 300 HV for both MAS. With decreasing penetration depth below 10 µm, a hardness increase to a maximum of 1100 HV and 650–900 HV for MAS 100 and 100Al, respectively, is observed. Fig. 8 Vickers hardness number in relation to the indentation depth of both MAS 100 (left) and MAS 100Al (right). Measurements were conducted directly on the worn surfaces using different hardness measuring loads: HV0.01 (0.0981 N), HV0.1 (0.981 N), HV1 (9.81 N) and HV10 (98.1 N)

These observations are supported by the nanoindentation measurements on the cross section displayed in Fig.  9 . Herein, the hardness values are additionally distinguished by the phases (categorization via ECCI according to 2.2 Sample characterization). Regardless of the applied wear load, the indentation hardness of the austenite decreases with increasing distance from the surface. At depths above 10–12 µm for MAS 100 and 6–8 µm for MAS 100Al, the indentation hardness of austenite is in the range of 7–8 GPa. Starting from these values, the hardness of the austenite increases toward the surface and reaches a maximum of about 12 GPa at approximately 2 µm. The hardness of the thermal martensite does not show a distinct variation with depth and is characterized by values between 12 and 16 GPa. In the vicinity of the surface—approximately up to 2 µm—no phases can be assigned. Within this unassignable layer, the hardness ranges between 12 and 18 GPa. Fig. 9 Results of nanoindentation hardness measurement on cross sections of MAS 100 and 100Al subjected to different wear loads

sections.heading: Identification and Characterization of the Unassignable Layer
paragraphs: The microstructure of the two MAS in their initial state consists of metastable austenite and a small fraction of thermal martensite. After abrasive wear, a subsurface layer of a few microns formed.

Despite ECCI provides high special resolution and sensitivity to crystallographic orientation and phase contrast, this region cannot be unambiguously assigned to either austenite or martensite due to the high density of deformation structures (Fig.  5 ). Therefore, this region is referred to as an “unassignable” layer.

MFM measurements revealed that this subsurface layer constitutes a homogeneous ferromagnetic layer extending a few micrometers in depth (Fig.  6 ), which is consistent with the presence of martensite reported by XRD studies [ 9 ,  10 ,  12 ]. Nanoindentation measurements further support this interpretation, as both the hardness values and the load–displacement curves within the subsurface layer closely resemble those of thermal martensite measurements (Fig.  3 ). While nanoindentation cannot independently resolve phase composition, it provides complementary mechanical evidence.

Taken together, the combined results from ECCI, MFM and nanoindentation provide converging evidence for the formation of a martensitic subsurface layer during abrasive wear. Given that none of those techniques provide enough special resolution to analyze the microstructural morphology of the unassignable layer, TEM revealed nanometer-scale grains and a high density of deformation-induced martensite in the near-surface region. Owing to the localized nature of TEM analysis, these observations are representative but not spatially exhaustive.

The wear load has no measurable influence on the thickness of the martensitic layer. However, it should be noted that the wear load was comparably small due to limitations of the abrasion tester (maximum load approx. 32 N). Consequently, the observed insensitivity to load may reflect the restricted testing load rather than an intrinsic material response. Possibly, higher loads are required to cause measurable differences in microstructure and mechanical properties and should be investigated.

sections.heading: Influence of Aluminum
paragraphs: The ECCI images in Fig.  5  present a smaller affected zone (subsurface layer + deformed region) for MAS 100Al, compared to MAS 100. Differences between the two alloys can also be found in the results of the hardness-depth profiles (Vickers and nanoindentation). The absolute Vickers hardness as well as the depth of the hardened region is lower for the aluminum containing steel as can be seen in Figs.  8  and  9 , respectively. The hardened region consists of deformed, cold worked austenite and deformation-induced martensite. Correspondingly, the hardness-depth profile represents the interplay of both hardening contributions. During wear, both MAS are exposed to the same stress profile. The depth at which work hardening takes place is limited to the depth at which the acting stress applied during wear is larger than the yield strength of the material. As aluminum increases the yield strength due to solid solution hardening [ 18 ], for the MAS 100Al, this criterion is only achieved down to lower depths and a reduced affected zone results. Additionally, aluminum reduces the thermodynamic stability of the austenite [ 19 ,  20 ]. It could thus be expected that mechanically induced martensite forms at lower stresses and consequently at (i) larger depths beneath the surface and (ii) in larger amounts. Therefore, the lower Vickers hardness of the Al-containing steel seems contradictory at first. However, the deformation-induced martensitic transformation requires prior martensite nuclei formation [ 13 ,  21 ,  22 ]. Due to the increased yield strength of the Al-containing MAS, the deformation of austenite is hindered, and the necessary dislocation structure for the initiation of the martensitic transformation will only form at higher stresses and thus lower depths. Additionally, aluminum increases the stacking fault energy which leads to narrower stacking faults and, therefore, to less stable martensite nuclei [ 23 ,  24 ]. Thus, although aluminum thermodynamically reduces austenite stability, the concurrent increase in yield strength and stacking fault energy kinetically suppresses martensite nucleation under the applied wear conditions, resulting in a shallower affected zone and lower near-surface hardness in MAS 100Al. As shown in the previous studies [ 9 ], post-wear XRD analysis revealed higher austenite fractions in Al-containing steels. This may be attributed to the thinner martensitic layer, as the XRD information depth (approximately 1.5–4 µm) exceeds the observed layer thickness in this study. This also explains the lower Vickers hardness values near the surface of MAS 100Al (Fig.  8 ): with a thinner affected zone, the softer underlying austenite has a greater influence on the measured hardness.

Near-surface mechanical performance is controlled by the interaction between work-hardened austenite and deformation-induced martensite. In MAS without aluminum, extensive austenite deformation promotes martensite formation, increasing hardness and dissipating energy through plastic deformation rather than material removal. Aluminum raises yield strength and stacking fault energy, limiting deformation, so more energy contributes to material removal, reducing wear resistance. This highlights a key alloy design trade-off: Balancing austenite deformability and martensitic transformation is critical to maximize energy dissipation and wear resistance in metastable austenitic steels.

sections.heading: Ductility in the Subsurface Layer
paragraphs: As shown in a previous investigation [ 9 ] as well as in Fig.  10 , the abraded surfaces are characterized by ridges and grooves indicating a partly ductile behavior, even though high-carbon martensite is known to be brittle [ 14 ,  15 ]. Fig. 10 SEM image of the surface of a MAS 100 sample subjected to abrasive wear at 24 N (part of unpublished data)

Chatterjee and Bhadeshia [ 25 ] stated that cracking or brittle behavior of high-carbon martensite occurs only above a critical size of the martensite plates. Thus, by refining the absolute size of the martensite by reducing the prior austenite grain size, cracking was prohibited.

Equation  2  shows the modified Griffith equation for calculating the fracture strength in dependence of the maximum martensite size, i.e., on the prior austenite grain size. Here,  γ S  is the surface energy of fracture ( γ S  = 100 J m −2  [ 27 ]) and  E  the Youngs modulus (E = 210 GPa).

In Fig.  11 , the calculated martensite yield strength for different carbon contents (0.6 − 1.2 wt%) and the fracture strength as a function of grain size are plotted. The intersection points of the  σ Y  and  σ F  curves represent the critical grain sizes. For a carbon content of 1 wt%, the calculated critical grain size is approximately 10 µm. For larger grains, brittle behavior is expected, for smaller values ductile behavior. Please note that this is only a rough estimate, since the equations and values used for the calculation were not specifically tailored for high-carbon steels nor mechanically induced martensite. Furthermore, possible deviations from classical Hall–Petch behavior, such as inverse Hall–Petch effects at very small grain sizes, are not explicitly considered. Nonetheless, this estimation aligns well with the findings of Chatterjee and Bhadeshia [ 25 ], who reported a critical martensite grain size of 10 µm for a steel with approximately 1 wt% C (Fe–0.98C–1.46Si–1.89Mn–1.26Cr–0.26Mo). Fig. 11 Estimated fracture and yield strength as a function of grain size for high-carbon martensite

As Fig.  7  displays, the subsurface layer consists of grains that are several nanometers in size, which are, therefore, well below the calculated critical size. As such, this grain size most likely lead to a ductile behavior within the subsurface layer. It is known from several investigations [ 13 ,  21 ], that martensite nuclei form strain-induced at junction points of deformation twins or shear-bands. As explained earlier, increasing strain leads to a progressive increase in the martensite fraction. The highest shear stresses occur just beneath the surface [ 29 ], resulting in a localized increase in dislocation density. Neog et al. [ 30 ] estimated equivalent strains of up to 3 in the near-surface region of bainitized steel under dry-sliding wear condition. With decreasing surface distance, the deformation structure density (dislocations, slip bands, deformation twins, deformation-induced martensite) increases, which leads to the above mentioned unassignable layer. Based on this, it is assumed that martensite nuclei form beneath the surface as a result of mechanical twin or micro shear band formation in the austenite due to the high local strains. Micro shear band formation or mechanical twins can be seen in sufficient depth below the surface in Fig.  5 . Because of the high dislocation density, many nuclei form simultaneously and, therefore, hinder growth of single martensite nuclei. This results in the nanostructured martensite featured in the TEM microstructures (Fig.  7 ).

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The microstructures and properties in the near-surface region of two MAS after abrasive wear have been studied. The following conclusions can be drawn: Abrasive wear induces a martensitic subsurface layer with a thickness of a few microns, with no significant dependence on the applied wear load. Nanoindentation hardness of austenite increases from 7.5–12 GPa in the near-surface region due to work hardening. 1.5 wt% aluminum reduces both the thickness of the martensitic layer and the depth of work-hardened austenite. During wear, the high density of near-surface deformation promotes extensive martensite nucleation, leading to nanometer-scale grain sizes and enabling ductile behavior, as confirmed by TEM.
